screens.title: Serverless CI/CD pipeline stages
screens.narratorSegment: A serverless CI/CD pipeline still follows the classic Source → Build → Test → Deploy stages, but the artifacts and actions differ because templates and function code must be packaged and versioned. Begin with a Source stage where your SAM or CDK project, Lambda handlers, and infrastructure templates live in version control. Commits trigger the pipeline. The Build stage runs sam build or cdk synth. This produces a CloudFormation template and packaged artifacts; CodeBuild also runs unit tests here to provide fast feedback. Build artifacts are typically the packaged template and zipped function code in S3. The Test stage runs integration and end-to-end tests against a deployed staging environment. Integration tests validate interactions with DynamoDB, SQS, or other services. End-to-end tests exercise the full A P I flow from triggering event to final state. Finally the Deploy stage uses CloudFormation and CodeDeploy to update stacks and manage Lambda versions and aliases so a stable alias references a version. A common misconception is to treat Lambda updates like container pushes; because Lambda allows immutable versions and aliases, you should publish versions and shift aliases rather than repeatedly patching the $LATEST entry. Example: a pipeline commits, CodeBuild runs sam build and unit tests, artifacts are packaged to S3, a staging deploy occurs for integration tests, and a production deploy uses CodeDeploy canary rules. Reflect: which stage would you run quick unit tests in, and why?

screens.title: Build stage: sam build, packaging, and artifacts
screens.narratorSegment: The Build stage converts your source into deployable artifacts. In a SAM project, CodeBuild typically runs sam build to assemble dependencies and then sam package to put function code into S3 and produce a packaged CloudFormation template. The build is also where you run unit tests for Lambda functions so failures are detected early. A common setup uses a buildspec. yaml file in the repo that installs the SAM CLI, runs sam build --template template. yaml and then sam package with your artifact S3 bucket. For example, the buildspec commands will install dependencies, invoke the test runner, and, on success, create packaged. yaml that CodePipeline will later reference. A misconception is to push raw code into deployment without packaging templates; this fails to capture dependency layers or proper S3 object references. Concrete example: CodeBuild runs sam build into. aws-sam/build, then sam package to produce packaged. yaml and uploads zipped functions to an artifacts S3 bucket. Ensure the CodeBuild service role has permissions to put objects in the S3 artifact bucket and to generate CloudFormation templates. Key practical tip: run unit tests before package steps to avoid packaging bad builds and to speed feedback loops.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Build stage: sam build, packaging, and artifacts
Build stage responsibilities
  • • Run sam build or cdk synth to assemble code and dependencies.
  • • Run unit tests to provide fast feedback and fail fast.
  • • Package artifacts with sam package into S3 and produce packaged.yaml.
  • • Produce build artifacts for deploy stage: packaged template and zipped function code.
Common mistake
Packaging after tests fail wastes time. Run unit tests before packaging and uploading artifacts.
Example buildspec.yaml
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      python: 3.9
    commands:
      - pip install aws-sam-cli
  build:
    commands:
      - echo "Building SAM application..."
      - sam build --template template.yaml --build-dir .aws-sam/build
      - sam package --template-file .aws-sam/build/template.yaml --s3-bucket <YOUR_ARTIFACT_BUCKET_NAME> --output-template-file packaged.yaml
  post_build:
    commands:
      - echo "Build and package complete."
artifacts:
  files:
    - packaged.yaml
Key Takeaway

Keep tests before packaging and ensure CodeBuild roles can write to the artifact S3 bucket so deploys reference correct artifacts.

screens.title: Test stage: unit, integration, and end-to-end tests
screens.narratorSegment: Testing serverless functions requires layered strategies. Unit tests exercise pure function logic locally with mocks for AWS clients so they run quickly during the Build stage. Use standard mocking frameworks such as the language-native mock libraries to simulate service responses; this keeps tests deterministic and fast. Integration tests validate how the function interacts with real services. For faster integration feedback you might use local emulation tools like moto for Python or sam local invoke with test events, but the most authoritative integration tests run against a deployed staging environment created by the pipeline. End-to-end tests exercise the full flow — for example, an A P I Gateway request that triggers a Lambda, writes to DynamoDB, and returns a response. These tests run in the Test stage after a staging deploy so you validate infrastructure wiring. A common misconception is to rely solely on unit tests; they miss integration issues like IAM permissions or misconfigured resources. Practical example: run unit tests in CodeBuild's build phase, deploy to a staging stack, then have a separate CodeBuild job or Lambda test runner invoke the A P I endpoints and assert expected behavior. Close by asking: which failure mode would you detect in unit tests, and which would only show up in integration tests?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Test stage: unit, integration, and end-to-end tests
Testing layers and when to run them
Unit tests: fast, isolated, use mocks. Integration tests: verify real service interactions. End-to-end: validate full user flow.
Unit tests
Run in CodeBuild during build. Mock AWS clients so logic is validated without network calls.
Integration tests
Run against a staging deploy or use local emulators like moto for faster cycles. Catch IAM and resource configuration issues.
End-to-end tests
Exercise triggers and downstream services in a staging environment to validate the full app flow.
Example scenario
A shopping API: unit tests validate price calculation logic. Integration tests verify DynamoDB writes succeed and permissions are correct. End-to-end tests simulate a create-order request that triggers workflows and confirms final state.
Common mistake

Relying only on unit tests misses configuration and permission errors that only appear when resources are deployed and wired together.

Pro Tip

Use a separate staging account or isolated stack to run integration tests without impacting production quotas or data.

screens.title: Observability: CloudWatch Logs, Metrics, and X-Ray
screens.narratorSegment: Observability gives you the data you need to make deployment decisions and to troubleshoot failures. Start with CloudWatch Logs: every Lambda invocation can emit structured logs; use JSON where possible so queries are easier. Log input events, key processing steps, and errors. Metrics are emitted automatically by Lambda — invocations, duration, errors, and throttles — and you should create CloudWatch dashboards and alarms on those metrics, for example alert when Errors > 0 or Throttles > 0. X-Ray adds distributed tracing: by instrumenting Lambda functions with the X-Ray SDK you capture subsegments showing calls to downstream services like DynamoDB or A P I Gateway. This gives an end-to-end view so you can see where latency or errors accumulate. A common misconception is that logs alone are sufficient; logs are necessary but traces give you the connected request path across services. Concrete example: if users report intermittent timeouts, dashboards may show increased duration metrics, but a trace can point to a specific downstream call that is slow. Key operational practice: feed CloudWatch alarms into CodeDeploy deployment preferences so canary decisions are made from the same signals you use for operational alerts.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Observability: CloudWatch Logs, Metrics, and X-Ray
Logging and metrics
Structured logs in CloudWatch and default Lambda metrics are your first line of observability. Create dashboards and alarms on Errors, Duration, and Throttles.
CloudWatch Logs
Emit JSON logs with request IDs, input event, and error context for faster querying.
CloudWatch Metrics
Use built-in metrics and create alarms to detect and react to failures during canary deploys.
Tracing with X-Ray
X-Ray shows the request path across API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and other services, letting you find bottlenecks and error origins.
Example
A trace shows that the second Lambda call waits on a slow DynamoDB query. Correlate trace ID and logs to see the exact request payload and timing.
Pro Tip

Use the same CloudWatch alarms for both operational alerts and deployment health checks so rollback decisions use production-grade signals.

screens.title: Lambda versions and aliases
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda versions provide immutable snapshots of your function code and configuration; every published version receives a unique identifier you can reference directly. Aliases are mutable pointers to those versions and provide a stable name, like Live or Prod, for external invocations. The typical workflow publishes a new version after the deploy, then updates an alias to point to that version. This lets you rollback by re-pointing the alias to a previous stable version. A common error is updating the Live alias directly to point at $LATEST; that loses immutability guarantees and makes rollbacks less reliable. With AutoPublishAlias in SAM you can have the deployment publish a version and assign an alias automatically. An example SAM fragment shows AutoPublishAlias: Live and DeploymentPreference: Canary10Percent5Minutes, which instructs CodeDeploy to use the alias for gradual traffic shifting. A practical scenario: you deploy version 3, CodeDeploy shifts 10 percent of traffic to version 3 while monitoring alarms, and if healthy, continues to 100 percent. If an alarm fires, CodeDeploy moves the alias back to the prior version. Think about why aliases are preferred for traffic control compared to addressing versions directly in routing rules.

keyIdea.title: Immutable versions, mutable aliases
keyIdea.text: Publish Lambda versions to capture immutable releases and use aliases to point clients at the desired version so deployments can shift traffic safely and be rolled back.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Lambda versions and aliases
Concepts
Publish an immutable version of your function code. Use aliases to reference versions and to shift production traffic safely.
Version
Immutable snapshot of code and configuration with its own ARN.
Alias
A pointer to a specific version that clients can invoke using a stable name.
Key Takeaway

Always publish versions and update aliases for production traffic so rollbacks remain predictable and auditable.

SAM template example
MyApiFunction:
  Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
  Properties:
    Handler: app.lambda_handler
    Runtime: python3.9
    CodeUri: ./my_api_function
    AutoPublishAlias: Live
    DeploymentPreference:
      Type: Canary10Percent5Minutes
      Alarms:
        - !GetAtt MyApiFunctionErrorsAlarm.Arn
        - !GetAtt MyApiFunctionInvocationsAlarm.Arn
This snippet demonstrates AutoPublishAlias and a canary deployment preference that ties into CloudWatch alarms to determine health during rollout.

screens.title: Canary deployments with CodeDeploy
screens.narratorSegment: Canary deployments let you introduce a new Lambda version to a small percentage of production traffic and validate its health before a full rollout. CodeDeploy integrates with Lambda aliases to manage this traffic shifting automatically. The process is: publish a new version, then update the alias so CodeDeploy routes a small share of traffic to the new version, for example ten percent for five minutes. During that period CodeDeploy monitors CloudWatch alarms you supplied, such as an Errors > 0 alarm or an Invocations drop alarm. If alarms remain clear, CodeDeploy increases traffic in steps until the alias points fully to the new version. If any alarm triggers, CodeDeploy rolls back the alias to the previous stable version automatically. A misconception is to think canaries replace testing; they complement testing by protecting production from unexpected regressions. For example, your deployment preference might be Canary10Percent5Minutes; CodeDeploy will shift 10 percent, evaluate alarms for 5 minutes, then continue. Another practical point: include both error and invocation-based alarms so silent failures or major traffic drops are detectable. Reflect: which alarms would you add to detect a silent failure where requests succeed but results are incorrect?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Canary deployments with CodeDeploy
Canary pattern
Shift a small percentage of traffic to a new version, monitor alarms, then continue or rollback automatically.
Step 1: Publish new Lambda version after deployment.
Step 2: CodeDeploy updates alias to route a percentage to new version.
Step 3: Alarms are monitored; if healthy, traffic increases; if not, rollback occurs.
Pro Tip

Use a mix of error rate and invocation-based alarms to detect both overt failures and silent regressions such as missing output or empty responses.

Example rollout plan
Canary10Percent5Minutes: shift 10% for 5 minutes, evaluate alarms, then proceed. CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes is a deploy config that matches this behavior.
Key Takeaway

Canaries give you a safety net: incremental exposure and automatic rollback keep production stable during change.

keyIdea.title: Template-driven deployment preferences
keyIdea.text: Add AutoPublishAlias and DeploymentPreference to your SAM function resources so CodeDeploy can perform alias-based canaries using your CloudWatch alarms.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › SAM template updates for CodeDeploy integration
What AutoPublishAlias and DeploymentPreference do
  • • AutoPublishAlias publishes an immutable version and points an alias at it.
  • • DeploymentPreference instructs CodeDeploy to perform canary or linear traffic shifting and to monitor specified alarms.
  • • Hooks let you run validation functions before or after traffic is shifted.
Common mistake

Not attaching alarms to DeploymentPreference removes automated safety checks and forces manual monitoring during a canary.

Template example (excerpt)
MyApiFunction:
  Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
  Properties:
    Handler: app.lambda_handler
    Runtime: python3.9
    CodeUri: ./my_api_function
    AutoPublishAlias: Live
    DeploymentPreference:
      Type: Canary10Percent5Minutes
      Hooks:
        PreTrafficHook: !Ref PreTrafficLambdaFunction
        PostTrafficHook: !Ref PostTrafficLambdaFunction
      Alarms:
        - !GetAtt MyApiFunctionErrorsAlarm.Arn
        - !GetAtt MyApiFunctionInvocationsAlarm.Arn
This configuration lets SAM and CodeDeploy coordinate to publish a version, run optional hooks, and shift traffic while checking alarms.

screens.title: Create CodePipeline and CodeBuild for SAM apps
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a pipeline for a SAM application involves configuring a source provider, a build provider, and a deploy provider in CodePipeline. Start by selecting GitHub or CodeCommit as the Source stage and point it at your repository branch. The Build stage uses CodeBuild; create a project with a managed image that includes your language runtime and install the SAM CLI in the buildspec. The buildspec we saw earlier installs aws-sam-cli, runs sam build, runs unit tests, packages artifacts to S3, and emits packaged. yaml as an output artifact. In the Deploy stage select AWS CloudFormation and provide the BuildArtifact::packaged. yaml as the template to create or update the stack. Be sure the CloudFormation action runs with a role that has permissions for Lambda, A P I Gateway, DynamoDB, CloudWatch, and CodeDeploy because the SAM template may create or update these resources. A common misconception is that the pipeline can run with full admin rights; instead, configure least-privilege roles for each service and ensure CodeBuild, CodePipeline, and CodeDeploy roles have only the permissions required. Example practical steps: create my-serverless-pipeline in the console, add source, add CodeBuild project my-serverless-build with the buildspec, then add a CloudFormation deploy action that uses CodeDeployDefault. LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes for deploy config.

  1. Source: GitHub or CodeCommit repository, branch selection.
  2. Build: CodeBuild project runs buildspec to build, test, and package.
  3. Test: optional separate integration tests against staging deploy.
  4. Deploy: CloudFormation action uses packaged.yaml and CodeDeploy for canaries.
Remember to choose the CloudFormation execution role with permissions to create/update all resources your SAM template defines. Also select a CodeDeploy deployment config such as CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes if you want canary behavior to match your DeploymentPreference.
Checklist for roles and artifacts
  • • CodeBuild service role can write artifacts to S3 and run sam commands.
  • • CloudFormation execution role can create/update Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, CloudWatch, CodeDeploy.
  • • CodeDeploy role can manage alias updates and monitor alarms.

screens.title: Deployment hooks and alarms
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment hooks provide a programmable way to validate a new Lambda version before or after traffic is shifted. You can register pre-traffic and post-traffic hooks as Lambda functions that CodeDeploy invokes during a canary. For example, a pre-traffic hook could run a quick integration smoke test against the new version and then call codedeploy. put_lifecycle_event_hook_execution_status to indicate success or failure. Post-traffic hooks might run final verification steps or trigger notifications. Alarms are equally important: CloudWatch alarms attached to DeploymentPreference tell CodeDeploy which metrics to observe during the rollout. The chapter shows alarms on Errors and Invocations for the Live alias — Errors > 0 or Invocations dropping to zero signals trouble. A common misconception is to use many noisy alarms; instead pick clear, high-signal metrics tied to correct behavior. Example: an error-count alarm with threshold zero helps detect any exception raises during the canary window. Hooks and alarms together provide both automated checks and human-readable signals. Practical tip: if your hook fails, CodeDeploy can stop the rollout and report the failure, allowing your pipeline to mark the deployment as unsuccessful and preventing further exposure.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Deployment hooks and alarms
Lifecycle hooks
Pre-traffic hooks let you run checks against the new version before traffic shifts. Post-traffic hooks validate after full or partial traffic shift. Hooks use the CodeDeploy lifecycle API to report success or failure.
Example hook behavior
A pre-traffic hook runs a small integration test. If it succeeds, it signals CodeDeploy to continue. If it fails, CodeDeploy stops the rollout and the alias remains pointed at the old version.
CloudWatch alarms
Attach high-signal alarms to DeploymentPreference, such as an Errors alarm (threshold zero) or an Invocations alarm that detects drops in traffic. CodeDeploy evaluates these alarms during the canary window.
Common mistake

Relying on verbose or noisy alarms can cause false rollbacks. Choose alarms that directly indicate degraded user experience.

screens.title: Permissions and secrets for safe automation
screens.narratorSegment: Security and permissions are central to a safe CI/CD pipeline. Pipeline IAM roles must have the permissions they need — no more — to reduce attack surface. For example, CodeBuild needs permission to run sam build and to write artifacts to the S3 artifact bucket. CodeDeploy needs permissions to update aliases and interact with deployment lifecycle APIs. CloudFormation needs rights to create or update the resources declared in the SAM template, including Lambda, A P I Gateway, DynamoDB, and CloudWatch alarms. A common mistake is giving overly broad permissions; follow least-privilege and grant only the fine-grained actions required, such as lambda:PublishVersion and lambda:UpdateAlias for deployment tasks. For sensitive configuration values, use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store and grant Lambda functions the permission to retrieve them at runtime. Also ensure your build and deploy roles can read the required parameters but not modify secrets. Practical example: define a CodeBuild role that includes s3:PutObject for the artifact bucket and limited CloudFormation permissions, and a CodeDeploy role with codedeploy:CreateDeployment and lambda:UpdateAlias. Reflect: which permission would you restrict to prevent accidental cross-account deployments?

keyIdea.title: Least-privilege pipeline roles
keyIdea.text: Grant only the permissions required for each pipeline component and use Secrets Manager or Parameter Store for sensitive configuration retrieval at runtime.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Permissions and secrets for safe automation
Role responsibilities
Map each role to the minimum actions it needs. Example roles: CodeBuild service role, CodePipeline role, CloudFormation execution role, CodeDeploy role, and Lambda execution roles.
• CodeBuild: s3:PutObject for artifact bucket, ability to run sam CLI.
• CloudFormation: permissions to create/update resources in your SAM template.
• CodeDeploy: lambda:UpdateAlias, codedeploy:CreateDeployment, codedeploy:PutLifecycleEventHookExecutionStatus for hooks.
Secrets and parameters
Store sensitive values in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store. Give Lambda functions read-only permission to retrieve them at runtime. Avoid embedding secrets in templates or code.
Key Takeaway

Define narrow roles per pipeline component and centralize secrets to limit exposure and make audits simpler.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core concepts to carry forward. First, serverless CI/CD is an automated pipeline that treats SAM/CDK templates and Lambda artifacts as deployable outputs; CodePipeline orchestrates source, build, test, and deploy stages. Second, AWS CodeBuild runs sam build and unit tests and prepares packaged templates and zipped Lambda artifacts for deployment. Third, a layered testing strategy matters: unit tests run fast with mocks, integration tests validate real service interactions, and end-to-end tests exercise full flows against staging. Fourth, observability with CloudWatch Logs and Metrics plus X-Ray tracing is necessary to detect, diagnose, and drive automated rollback decisions. Fifth, Lambda versions are immutable snapshots and aliases are pointers that provide a stable endpoint; CodeDeploy uses aliases to perform canary rollouts. Finally, use deployment hooks and CloudWatch alarms to validate during canaries and follow least-privilege IAM practices and secure secret management. These concepts form a coherent workflow that enables rapid releases while minimizing production risk.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to build a resilient CI/CD and operations workflow for serverless applications. We'll treat Lambda code, SAM or CDK templates, and deployment configuration as first-class artifacts in the pipeline so you can automate build, test, and safe rollout. You will see how CodeCommit or GitHub, CodeBuild, CodePipeline and CodeDeploy work together with SAM to publish immutable Lambda versions and use aliases to shift traffic gradually. We'll also cover testing strategies — unit, integration, and end-to-end — and why each matters for fast feedback. Observability is central: CloudWatch Logs and Metrics give you the raw data, while X-Ray provides request-level traces across functions and services. Finally, you'll learn how canary deployments reduce risk by shifting traffic and enabling automatic rollbacks triggered by CloudWatch alarms. As an example, a small A P I backed by DynamoDB can be packaged with sam build, packaged to S3, then deployed through CodePipeline; each deployment publishes a version and updates a Live alias that CodeDeploy can move from 0 to 100 percent while monitoring alarms. By the end, you’ll understand the pieces required to ship changes rapidly while keeping production safe.

First, you'll learn to design and implement CI/CD pipelines specifically for serverless applications. That means treating SAM or CDK templates and Lambda artifacts as deployable outputs and orchestrating source, build, test, and deploy stages using AWS Developer Tools. For example, you'll create a pipeline that runs sam build, packages artifacts to S3, and triggers CloudFormation deploys. Second, you will automate testing strategies for Lambda: write unit tests with mocking to validate pure function logic, and set up integration tests against a staging environment so you can catch service interactions early. Both skills reduce defects and speed delivery. Third, learn to instrument Lambda with CloudWatch Logs and Metrics, create dashboards and alarms, and use X-Ray for request tracing. Observability makes rollouts safe because alarms drive rollback rules. Finally, you will manage Lambda versions and aliases and apply canary deployments via CodeDeploy. This gives you immutable versions and a stable invocation pointer that allows gradual traffic shifting and automatic rollback on alarm conditions. Each objective ties directly to operational safety and faster iteration.

This second objectives slide focuses on the technical practices you'll use daily. You'll learn to integrate AWS Developer Tools like CodeBuild and CodePipeline with SAM or CDK so builds run sam build and produce packaged CloudFormation templates ready for deployment. You'll design testing stages that run unit tests during build and separate integration or end-to-end tests against a staging environment. Another objective is to manage deployment safety: publish immutable Lambda versions and create aliases such as Live or Prod to provide a stable invocation point. Then automate canary deployments using CodeDeploy and CloudWatch alarms so the pipeline can shift a small percentage of traffic to a new version, watch metrics and errors, and either progress or roll back automatically. Finally, you'll practice least-privilege IAM for pipeline roles and learn where to store secrets with Parameter Store or Secrets Manager. Each objective maps to a concrete action in the hands-on activity, preparing you to implement a pipeline that actually promotes safely from source to production.

A serverless CI/CD pipeline still follows the classic Source → Build → Test → Deploy stages, but the artifacts and actions differ because templates and function code must be packaged and versioned. Begin with a Source stage where your SAM or CDK project, Lambda handlers, and infrastructure templates live in version control. Commits trigger the pipeline. The Build stage runs sam build or cdk synth. This produces a CloudFormation template and packaged artifacts; CodeBuild also runs unit tests here to provide fast feedback. Build artifacts are typically the packaged template and zipped function code in S3. The Test stage runs integration and end-to-end tests against a deployed staging environment. Integration tests validate interactions with DynamoDB, SQS, or other services. End-to-end tests exercise the full A P I flow from triggering event to final state. Finally the Deploy stage uses CloudFormation and CodeDeploy to update stacks and manage Lambda versions and aliases so a stable alias references a version. A common misconception is to treat Lambda updates like container pushes; because Lambda allows immutable versions and aliases, you should publish versions and shift aliases rather than repeatedly patching the $LATEST entry. Example: a pipeline commits, CodeBuild runs sam build and unit tests, artifacts are packaged to S3, a staging deploy occurs for integration tests, and a production deploy uses CodeDeploy canary rules. Reflect: which stage would you run quick unit tests in, and why?

The Build stage converts your source into deployable artifacts. In a SAM project, CodeBuild typically runs sam build to assemble dependencies and then sam package to put function code into S3 and produce a packaged CloudFormation template. The build is also where you run unit tests for Lambda functions so failures are detected early. A common setup uses a buildspec. yaml file in the repo that installs the SAM CLI, runs sam build --template template. yaml and then sam package with your artifact S3 bucket. For example, the buildspec commands will install dependencies, invoke the test runner, and, on success, create packaged. yaml that CodePipeline will later reference. A misconception is to push raw code into deployment without packaging templates; this fails to capture dependency layers or proper S3 object references. Concrete example: CodeBuild runs sam build into. aws-sam/build, then sam package to produce packaged. yaml and uploads zipped functions to an artifacts S3 bucket. Ensure the CodeBuild service role has permissions to put objects in the S3 artifact bucket and to generate CloudFormation templates. Key practical tip: run unit tests before package steps to avoid packaging bad builds and to speed feedback loops.

Testing serverless functions requires layered strategies. Unit tests exercise pure function logic locally with mocks for AWS clients so they run quickly during the Build stage. Use standard mocking frameworks such as the language-native mock libraries to simulate service responses; this keeps tests deterministic and fast. Integration tests validate how the function interacts with real services. For faster integration feedback you might use local emulation tools like moto for Python or sam local invoke with test events, but the most authoritative integration tests run against a deployed staging environment created by the pipeline. End-to-end tests exercise the full flow — for example, an A P I Gateway request that triggers a Lambda, writes to DynamoDB, and returns a response. These tests run in the Test stage after a staging deploy so you validate infrastructure wiring. A common misconception is to rely solely on unit tests; they miss integration issues like IAM permissions or misconfigured resources. Practical example: run unit tests in CodeBuild's build phase, deploy to a staging stack, then have a separate CodeBuild job or Lambda test runner invoke the A P I endpoints and assert expected behavior. Close by asking: which failure mode would you detect in unit tests, and which would only show up in integration tests?

Observability gives you the data you need to make deployment decisions and to troubleshoot failures. Start with CloudWatch Logs: every Lambda invocation can emit structured logs; use JSON where possible so queries are easier. Log input events, key processing steps, and errors. Metrics are emitted automatically by Lambda — invocations, duration, errors, and throttles — and you should create CloudWatch dashboards and alarms on those metrics, for example alert when Errors > 0 or Throttles > 0. X-Ray adds distributed tracing: by instrumenting Lambda functions with the X-Ray SDK you capture subsegments showing calls to downstream services like DynamoDB or A P I Gateway. This gives an end-to-end view so you can see where latency or errors accumulate. A common misconception is that logs alone are sufficient; logs are necessary but traces give you the connected request path across services. Concrete example: if users report intermittent timeouts, dashboards may show increased duration metrics, but a trace can point to a specific downstream call that is slow. Key operational practice: feed CloudWatch alarms into CodeDeploy deployment preferences so canary decisions are made from the same signals you use for operational alerts.

Lambda versions provide immutable snapshots of your function code and configuration; every published version receives a unique identifier you can reference directly. Aliases are mutable pointers to those versions and provide a stable name, like Live or Prod, for external invocations. The typical workflow publishes a new version after the deploy, then updates an alias to point to that version. This lets you rollback by re-pointing the alias to a previous stable version. A common error is updating the Live alias directly to point at $LATEST; that loses immutability guarantees and makes rollbacks less reliable. With AutoPublishAlias in SAM you can have the deployment publish a version and assign an alias automatically. An example SAM fragment shows AutoPublishAlias: Live and DeploymentPreference: Canary10Percent5Minutes, which instructs CodeDeploy to use the alias for gradual traffic shifting. A practical scenario: you deploy version 3, CodeDeploy shifts 10 percent of traffic to version 3 while monitoring alarms, and if healthy, continues to 100 percent. If an alarm fires, CodeDeploy moves the alias back to the prior version. Think about why aliases are preferred for traffic control compared to addressing versions directly in routing rules.

Canary deployments let you introduce a new Lambda version to a small percentage of production traffic and validate its health before a full rollout. CodeDeploy integrates with Lambda aliases to manage this traffic shifting automatically. The process is: publish a new version, then update the alias so CodeDeploy routes a small share of traffic to the new version, for example ten percent for five minutes. During that period CodeDeploy monitors CloudWatch alarms you supplied, such as an Errors > 0 alarm or an Invocations drop alarm. If alarms remain clear, CodeDeploy increases traffic in steps until the alias points fully to the new version. If any alarm triggers, CodeDeploy rolls back the alias to the previous stable version automatically. A misconception is to think canaries replace testing; they complement testing by protecting production from unexpected regressions. For example, your deployment preference might be Canary10Percent5Minutes; CodeDeploy will shift 10 percent, evaluate alarms for 5 minutes, then continue. Another practical point: include both error and invocation-based alarms so silent failures or major traffic drops are detectable. Reflect: which alarms would you add to detect a silent failure where requests succeed but results are incorrect?

To integrate CodeDeploy canaries with your Lambda resources, update your SAM template to include AutoPublishAlias and DeploymentPreference. AutoPublishAlias tells SAM to publish a version automatically when the function code changes and to create or update an alias such as Live. DeploymentPreference configures how CodeDeploy should shift traffic to that alias and which CloudWatch alarms to monitor during the rollout. The template snippet in the chapter shows MyApiFunction with AutoPublishAlias: Live and a DeploymentPreference that uses Canary10Percent5Minutes and references alarms such as MyApiFunctionErrorsAlarm and MyApiFunctionInvocationsAlarm. Hooks are optional pre- and post-traffic functions that can perform validation or notify CodeDeploy of hook status. A key misconception is to omit alarms; without them CodeDeploy cannot make health-based decisions. Creating a pipeline for a SAM application involves configuring a source provider, a build provider, and a deploy provider in CodePipeline. Deployment hooks provide a programmable way to validate a new Lambda version before or after traffic is shifted. You can register pre-traffic and post-traffic hooks as Lambda functions that CodeDeploy invokes during a canary. For example, a pre-traffic hook could run a quick integration smoke test against the new version and then call codedeploy. put_lifecycle_event_hook_execution_status to indicate success or failure. Post-traffic hooks might run final verification steps or trigger notifications. Alarms are equally important: CloudWatch alarms attached to DeploymentPreference tell CodeDeploy which metrics to observe during the rollout. The chapter shows alarms on Errors and Invocations for the Live alias — Errors > 0 or Invocations dropping to zero signals trouble. A common misconception is to use many noisy alarms; instead pick clear, high-signal metrics tied to correct behavior. Example: an error-count alarm with threshold zero helps detect any exception raises during the canary window. Hooks and alarms together provide both automated checks and human-readable signals. Practical tip: if your hook fails, CodeDeploy can stop the rollout and report the failure, allowing your pipeline to mark the deployment as unsuccessful and preventing further exposure.

Security and permissions are central to a safe CI/CD pipeline. Pipeline IAM roles must have the permissions they need — no more — to reduce attack surface. For example, CodeBuild needs permission to run sam build and to write artifacts to the S3 artifact bucket. CodeDeploy needs permissions to update aliases and interact with deployment lifecycle APIs. CloudFormation needs rights to create or update the resources declared in the SAM template, including Lambda, A P I Gateway, DynamoDB, and CloudWatch alarms. A common mistake is giving overly broad permissions; follow least-privilege and grant only the fine-grained actions required, such as lambda:PublishVersion and lambda:UpdateAlias for deployment tasks. For sensitive configuration values, use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store and grant Lambda functions the permission to retrieve them at runtime. Also ensure your build and deploy roles can read the required parameters but not modify secrets. Practical example: define a CodeBuild role that includes s3:PutObject for the artifact bucket and limited CloudFormation permissions, and a CodeDeploy role with codedeploy:CreateDeployment and lambda:UpdateAlias. Let's summarize the core concepts to carry forward. First, serverless CI/CD is an automated pipeline that treats SAM/CDK templates and Lambda artifacts as deployable outputs; CodePipeline orchestrates source, build, test, and deploy stages. Second, AWS CodeBuild runs sam build and unit tests and prepares packaged templates and zipped Lambda artifacts for deployment. Third, a layered testing strategy matters: unit tests run fast with mocks, integration tests validate real service interactions, and end-to-end tests exercise full flows against staging. Fourth, observability with CloudWatch Logs and Metrics plus X-Ray tracing is necessary to detect, diagnose, and drive automated rollback decisions. Fifth, Lambda versions are immutable snapshots and aliases are pointers that provide a stable endpoint; CodeDeploy uses aliases to perform canary rollouts. Finally, use deployment hooks and CloudWatch alarms to validate during canaries and follow least-privilege IAM practices and secure secret management. These concepts form a coherent workflow that enables rapid releases while minimizing production risk.

CodeBuild performs sam build, runs unit tests, and prepares packaged templates. CodeDeploy integrates with Lambda aliases to run canary deployments that obey CloudWatch alarms. Unit tests use mocking libraries to isolate logic, integration tests exercise real service interactions, and end-to-end tests validate the full flow. Use AutoPublishAlias and DeploymentPreference in SAM templates to publish versions and configure canaries. Finally, protect secrets in Parameter Store or Secrets Manager and configure IAM roles with least privilege. Remember: these are not optional extras but the mechanisms that let you automate safe rollouts and respond quickly to issues detected in production environments.
